items.question: How many bytes is `Zürich €` in UTF-8? (The gap is one space.)

feedback.correct: 11: five plain letters, `ü` takes 2, the space 1 and `€` 3.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Give each character its UTF-8 byte count and add them up.

byKey.chars: That is the number of characters. `ü` and `€` take more than one byte each.
byKey.euro-two: You gave `€` two bytes. U+20AC is above U+07FF, so it takes 3.

explain.text: Z, r, i, c, h and the space are 1 byte each, `ü` (U+00FC) is 2 and `€` (U+20AC) is 3. That makes $6 + 2 + 3 = 11$ bytes.

items.question: Which byte sequence decodes as UTF-8 without an error?

options.why: `c3` promises one continuation byte of the form `10xxxxxx`, but `28` is `00101000`.
`a9` is a continuation byte, so it cannot start a character.
`f0` starts a four-byte character, and only three bytes are here.

feedback.correct: `e2 82 ac` is a complete three-byte character, `€`.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Check each first byte's promise against the bytes that follow.

explain.text: `e2` is `1110xxxx`, so two continuation bytes must follow; `82` and `ac` both start `10`. The others start with a continuation byte, break a promise or stop short.

items.question: Train our BPE on `abab ab` until no pair appears twice. How many tokens is the text then?

feedback.generic: Not quite. Make the first merge, then count pairs again.

byKey.bytes: That is the byte count, before any merge.
byKey.merged-all: After `ab` is merged, every pair of the new row appears once, so training stops: no second merge.

explain.text: `ab` appears 3 times and becomes id 256, giving `256 256 space 256`. Every pair there appears once, so training stops at 4 tokens.

items.prose: Train our BPE on `xyxyz xyz`. The first merge is `xy`, which appears 3 times.
items.question: What is the second merge?

options.why: You counted on the original bytes, where `yz` appears twice. After the first merge every `y` sits inside `xy`.
That pair appears once, at the start.

feedback.correct: `xy` then `z` appears twice in the new row, so it becomes `xyz`.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Recount the pairs on the row after the first merge.

explain.text: After merge 1 the row is `xy xy z space xy z`. The pair `xy` then `z` appears twice and every other pair once, so merge 2 makes `xyz`.

items.prose: A tokeniser learned three merges, in this order: 256 is `a n`, 257 is `n a`, 258 is 256 followed by `a`.
items.question: How many tokens does it make of `banana`?

feedback.generic: Not quite. Apply the merges in the order learned.

byKey.na-first: You applied `n a` first. Merge 256 comes first and uses up both `n`s, so 257 never fires.
byKey.bytes: That is the byte count, before any merge.

explain.text: 256 turns `banana` into `b an an a`; 257 finds no free `n a`; 258 joins the last `an` and `a`. That leaves `b`, `an`, `ana`: 3 tokens.

items.prose: A model scores 3.6 nats per token on a set of annual reports. On those reports its tokeniser averages 4.1 bytes per token.
items.question: What is the loss in bits per byte? Give 4 decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Divide by the bytes per token, then by $\ln 2$.

byKey.nats-byte: That is nats per byte. Divide by $\ln 2$ to get bits.
byKey.bits-token: That is bits per token. Spread it over the 4.1 bytes each token covers.

explain.text: Per byte the loss is $3.6 / 4.1$ nats; dividing by $\ln 2$ turns nats into bits. So $3.6 / (4.1 \ln 2) \approx 1.2668$.

items.prose: A byte-level BPE tokeniser was trained on English text only. It meets `日本`, two characters of 3 bytes each.
items.question: What happens?

options.why: A byte-level tokeniser has no unknown token: every byte is in its vocabulary.
No merge joins these bytes, since none was learned from English text.

options.text: An error when it is encoded
options.why: Any string encodes to UTF-8 bytes, and all 256 bytes are tokens.

feedback.correct: Six byte tokens, and a perfect round trip.
feedback.generic: Not quite. What does a byte-level tokeniser fall back on?

explain.text: No learned merge touches these bytes, so each of the 6 bytes is its own token. Decoding joins them back into `日本`.

items.prose: A crawl of company websites gives 2 million pages. Every page carries the same cookie notice and menu lines, and some pages were fetched twice.
items.question: Which cleaning step removes the true duplicates and keeps every page's own content?

options.text: Deduplicate pages, and strip shared boilerplate separately
Delete every line that has appeared before
options.why: That deletes the shared lines from every page but the first. It also deletes repeated lines inside pages, such as headings.

options.text: Keep everything: duplicates do no harm
options.why: Pages fetched twice are trained on twice, and repeated text is memorised.

feedback.correct: Duplicates are found at the page level; shared boilerplate is a separate filter.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Pick the unit at which a repeat means the same content twice.

explain.text: A page fetched twice is a true duplicate, so compare whole pages. Lines repeated across pages are boilerplate, which a separate step strips.

items.prose: Two shingle sets: $A$ has 40 shingles, $B$ has 50, and 30 are in both.
items.question: What is their Jaccard similarity? Give a decimal.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Divide the shared shingles by the union.

byKey.over-a: You divided by $A$ alone. Jaccard divides by the union.
byKey.over-sum: You divided by $40 + 50$, which counts the 30 shared shingles twice.

items.prose: A filter flags two texts as near duplicates when their 5-character shingle sets have Jaccard similarity 0.9 or more. Two headlines of 67 characters differ in one digit: `Ashby Copper shares fall 4% after quarterly output misses forecasts`, and the same with 6%. Each has 63 distinct shingles.
items.question: What is their Jaccard similarity? Give 4 decimal places.

feedback.correct: $58 / 68 \approx 0.8529$, below 0.9, so the filter keeps both.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Count the shingles that cover the changed digit.

byKey.one-broken: You let the changed digit break one shingle. Every 5-character shingle that covers it breaks: 5 of them.
byKey.over-a: You divided by one headline's 63 shingles. Use the union.

explain.text: The digit sits inside 5 shingles of each headline, so 58 are shared and 68 are in either. $J = 58 / 68 \approx 0.8529$, below 0.9: one change costs a short text more of its overlap.
